notes.1a: This question was relatively well attempted. Many candidates successfully found correct values for the unbiased estimate of the population mean and variance. Only a few candidates found the biased estimate of the population variance. The confidence interval was often successfully found though errors were seen including the use of an incorrect z value.
notes.1b: Some candidates correctly stated the answer of 38 by finding 95 per cent of 40. Others incorrectly found 5 per cent or 97.5 per cent of 40 and some did not know what was required.
notes.2: Many candidates found this part to be challenging. When setting up the hypotheses, p should have been used; many candidates used Âµ or x. Few candidates found the correct binomial expression, and few made a valid comparison. Many candidates just calculated P(X = 5) or used incorrect values of p and q in their binomial expression. Others attempted to use a normal distribution or a Poisson distribution. After clearly showing a valid comparison, the conclusion should have been written in context and with a level of uncertainty in the language used.
notes.3: Some candidates successfully found the required probability, but errors were often made, particularly when finding the variance. Standardising was generally well attempted, but not all candidates found the correct probability region. A common error was giving an answer greater than 0.5 rather than less than 0.5 and this could have been avoided by drawing a diagram.
notes.4a: Many candidates realised that the need to find the mean and variance of both X and Y from the distributions given. Many of them then found E(X â€“ 3Y) successfully, but made errors when finding Var(X â€“ 3Y), for example using 3 rather than 32 or subtracting rather than adding in the formula. The question asked for the standard deviation; many candidates left their final answer as the variance. Candidates need to read the question carefully.
notes.4b: Many candidates found this part to be particularly challenging, with many candidates not realising that they needed to consider X = 0, Y = 0 and X = 1, Y = 15. Many tried incorrectly to work with a normal distribution and others were unable to make a start on the question.
notes.5a: This part was well attempted, with many candidates successfully finding the correct value for Î» and using a correct expression (which should be fully shown) to find the required probability. Errors included using an incorrect value for Î» or omitting a term in their Poisson expression.
notes.5b: This part was not quite as well attempted, though many candidates used N(162, 162) and many attempted to standardise. Some candidates omitted to use a continuity correction or used incorrect ones. Attempting to find the required probability (the area between two z values) was not straightforward for some.
notes.5c: The correct value for Î» was 4.65, but some candidates did not find this value and instead used 2.4 (the value just for the trucks). Candidates are advised to read the question carefully. In this case, the probability of cars and trucks arriving in the 10-minute period was required. Those who successfully found Î» usually went on to find the correct Poisson expression. Candidates with an incorrect value for Î» were able to gain some credit for use of a relevant Poisson expression. It is important that this expression is fully shown.
notes.6a: Some candidates realised that the median was , but a large number tried to find the median by integration. Some were successful but many did not use a correct expression for f(x).
notes.6b: Some candidates realised that the required probability was , but again many tried to find this probability by integration. A diagram may have helped candidates here.
notes.6c: In this part candidates needed to realise that f(x) was . Of those candidates who had this correct expression, many successfully found the variance. notes.6d: Very few candidates were successful in this part, and a significant number made no attempt at all. notes.7a: When stating hypotheses, it is important to be precise. Candidates should state â€˜population meanâ€™ (not just mean) or Âµ. Errors included use of 27 rather than 28.2 or a mixture of these, and use of x rather than Âµ.
notes.7b: A good number of candidates made a successful attempt at finding the probability of a Type I error. Many candidates standardised correctly and found the correct probability, though occasionally the 40 was omitted when standardising.
notes.7c: Some candidates realised that they needed to find the conclusion drawn from the information given, i.e., that H would not be rejected. The question asked if it would be possible to make a Type I or a Type II error or both. Many candidates merely said a Type II error could be made but did not say that a Type I could not. It is important for candidates to read the question carefully and answer it fully.
notes.key_messages:
It is important for candidates to read the questions carefully.
Drawing a sketch or diagram can often help candidates to understand and apply the information given in the
question.
For an answer to be fully correct, it needs to be supported by clear working, as stated in the rubric on the
question paper.
In a hypothesis test, the conclusion should be written in the context of the question. It should use appropriate
language with a degree of uncertainty, and it should not contain any contradiction.
